title: Tener vs Haber: Have, Has and There Is in Spanish
seo_title: Tener vs Haber: Have, Has and There Is in Spanish
meta_description: Tener vs haber: tener means to have (possess), haber builds perfect tenses and hay means there is. Clear rules, tener que vs hay que, mistakes and a quiz.

body_html:
Tener vs haber confuses learners because both can translate as “have”. But they do completely different jobs. Tener means “to have” in the sense of possessing or holding: Tengo dos hermanos. Haber is an auxiliary verb that builds perfect tenses (He comido, I have eaten), and in the form hay it means “there is” or “there are”. Once you see these three jobs, the confusion disappears.

Quick answer
  • Tener = to have, own, hold: Tengo un carro.
  • Haber + past participle = perfect tenses: He visto la película.
  • Hay = there is / there are: Hay un problema.
  • Tener que = to have to (personal); hay que = one has to (general).
{{toc}}

Tener vs haber: three different jobs

JobVerbExample
PossessiontenerTenemos una casa en el campo. We have a house in the country.
Perfect tenses (auxiliary)haberHan llegado. They have arrived.
Existencehay (haber)Hay mucha gente. There are a lot of people.
Personal obligationtener queTengo que trabajar. I have to work.
General obligationhay queHay que reciclar. One must recycle.

The RAE’s Diccionario panhispánico de dudas explains that haber in modern Spanish works mainly as an auxiliary and as an impersonal verb of existence; possession belongs to tener.

Tener: possession and much more

  • Tengo dos gatos. I have two cats.
  • ¿Tienes tiempo? Do you have time?
  • Tiene los ojos verdes. She has green eyes.

Tener also replaces English “be” in many expressions: tener hambre, tener frío, tener 30 años, tener razón, tener miedo. I list these in {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes in Spanish}}.

Haber as an auxiliary: “have done”

To say what you have done, use haber + past participle. Never tener:

  • He terminado. I have finished.
  • ¿Has estado en Perú? Have you been to Peru?
  • Habíamos salido. We had left.
  • Habrá llegado. He’ll have arrived (probably).

Present forms: he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han. The participle never changes: Ella ha comido, not comida.

{{image:2}}

Hay: there is, there are

Hay is the impersonal form of haber, and it is the same for singular and plural:

  • Hay un banco cerca. There’s a bank nearby.
  • Hay tres bancos cerca. There are three banks nearby.
  • ¿Hay leche? Is there any milk?

Other tenses stay singular too: había (there was/were), hubo, habrá, ha habido. So Había muchas personas, not habían, in standard Spanish, even though the plural is common in speech in many countries.

Hay vs está

Use hay to introduce something new (Hay un museo en la plaza), and estar to locate something specific (El museo está en la plaza). See {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser vs estar}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Tener que vs hay que

  • Tengo que estudiar. I have to study (me, personally).
  • Hay que estudiar para aprobar. You have to study to pass (anyone, in general).
  • Tenemos que irnos. We have to go.
  • Hay que tener paciencia. One needs patience.

And never haber que with a person: Yo hay que trabajar is wrong.

Real conversations

  • A: ¿Has comido? Hay enchiladas en el refri. (Have you eaten? There are enchiladas in the fridge.)
  • B: No, pero no tengo hambre. Tengo que salir ya. (No, but I’m not hungry. I have to go now.)
  • A: Bueno, pero hay que comer algo, ¿eh? (Okay, but you need to eat something, alright?)

A quick mental shortcut

If you can replace “have” with “own” or “hold”, use tener. If “have” is followed by a past participle (have eaten, have seen, have been), use haber. If English says “there is” or “there are”, use hay. One sentence holds all three: He visto que hay un departamento libre, pero no tengo dinero (I’ve seen that there’s an apartment available, but I don’t have money).

Regional notes

In everyday speech across Latin America and parts of Spain, you will often hear habían muchas personas or hubieron problemas, with plural agreement. It is very widespread, but the RAE recommends the singular, and it is safer in writing and exams. Also note that Spain uses the present perfect (hoy he comido paella) much more than most of Latin America, where the simple past is preferred for recent events (hoy comí paella).

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Tengo comido.He comido.Perfect tenses use haber
He dos hermanos.Tengo dos hermanos.Possession uses tener
Hay el libro en la mesa.El libro está en la mesa.Specific things use estar
Están tres personas. (there are)Hay tres personas.Existence uses hay
Ella ha comida.Ella ha comido.Participle doesn’t agree
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. There are two bathrooms. (Hay dos baños.)
  2. Have you seen my keys? (¿Has visto mis llaves?)
  3. I have a question. (Tengo una pregunta.)
  4. We have to leave early. (Tenemos que salir temprano.)
  5. You have to book in advance. (Hay que reservar con antelación.)

Don’t confuse haber with a ver: see {{link:haber-vs-a-ver|haber vs a ver}}. For more pairs, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Own it: tener. Have done it: haber. It exists: hay. Add tener que for your obligations and hay que for everyone’s, and you have, and have mastered, this pair.

faq.q: What is the difference between tener and haber?
faq.a: Tener means to have or possess. Haber is the auxiliary verb for perfect tenses (he comido) and, as hay, means there is or there are.

faq.q: Is it tengo comido or he comido?
faq.a: He comido. Perfect tenses always use haber + past participle.

faq.q: What is the difference between tener que and hay que?
faq.a: Tener que expresses a personal obligation (tengo que trabajar). Hay que expresses a general one (hay que trabajar para vivir).
